title_zh: 一袋面粉怎样穿过制裁
title_en: How a Bag of Flour Gets Through Sanctions
deck_zh: 石油可以卖，收入却要经过托管；食品可以进，生活却不只需要食品。从石油换食品计划，看共同决定怎样走到普通人的饭桌，又有没有一条路能从饭桌走回决定。
deck_en: Oil could be sold, but its revenue went through an escrow account. Food could enter, but a life requires more than food. Following the route to an Iraqi kitchen raises another question: what route led back from the kitchen to the decision?
body_zh: 1997年3月，石油换食品计划下的首批食品运抵伊拉克。这个名字听起来像一场直接交换：石油出去，粮食进来。真正的路却长得多。[1]
石油先要获准出口，收入进入联合国管理的托管账户，采购申请要经过相应程序，货物再运入和分发。它主要花的是伊拉克出售石油所得的钱，不是把外部捐来的粮食发下去那么简单。[3]
沿这条路看一袋面粉，我们会遇到几个不同的问题：谁让它可以进来，谁决定钱怎样用，谁负责把它送到，还有谁能在它迟到、缺少或不能解决生活困难时，要求重新看一看最初的安排。
面粉到了，是一件重要的事。但一项安排能把食品送进来，与受安排影响的人能把自己的问题送回去，并不是同一件事。
## 禁令写给国家，影响走进生活
这段历史不能从伊拉克只是被制裁的一方写起。1990年8月，伊拉克入侵科威特。8月6日，安理会依据《联合国宪章》第七章通过第661号决议，以贸易与资金限制迫使伊拉克遵守撤军要求、恢复科威特合法政府的权力。制裁有一个不能略去的起因：一个国家以武力侵犯了邻国。[2]
决议要求各国阻止规定范围内的贸易和资源供给，同时保留严格医疗用途物资的例外，食品则在人道情形下获得例外。它不是一份字面上禁止任何药物、任何食物进入的命令。可写有例外，与医院和家庭实际上取得所需物资，中间仍隔着钱、许可、运输和设施。[2]
命令没有停在纽约。各国要在自己能够控制的贸易、支付和运输环节落实限制。共同决定的约束，正是沿这些具体行动进入现实；不能因为最后关口由各国把守，就把国际层的决定说成没有作用。
同样，执行者也不是没有位置。某一项限制从哪里来，国内怎样实施，哪些物资可以批准，哪一处出现延误，需要分别追查。共同来源不替每一项执行自动免责，国内执行也不使共同设计从此不必回答。
1991年战争之后，联合国派出的跨机构调查团已警告严重人道灾难的危险。那一年提出过让伊拉克有限出售石油、支付人道需要的办法，伊拉克政府没有接受。后来1995年的第986号决议建立石油换食品计划，直到1996年达成实施安排并开始出口石油，食品才在次年到达。[3]
这些日期中间，不是空白。后来有了方案，不表示早年的困难都及时得到处理；政府拒绝过方案，也不能被剪掉，好把一切写成只有一方作出选择。要谈谁该做得不同，得先让每一方已经作过的决定留在图里。
对希望不再发动战争、又不能对侵略无所作为的人而言，经济压力有它的理由。这个理由值得认真对待。但不用炸弹，不等于没有生活成本；是否形成压力，与压力主要由谁承受，还须分开看。
## 有了食物，还缺什么
托管账户把一部分石油收入接到人道进口上，也为用途设置控制。中南部由伊拉克政府实施分发并接受联合国观察，北部三个省则由联合国实施计划。说成整个国家的粮食都由同一个机构以同一种方式送到，会把真正的责任分工说错。[3]
收入、批准、到货，也不是同一个数字。联合国在2003年的项目总结里区分已获批准的合同、已经抵达的物资与仍在生产运输途中的供应，并说明收入受到石油价格与出口条件影响。一份批准不能当成一袋已经发到手里的面粉。[1]
后来合同审查的办法也有变化。2002年新程序启用后，送交制裁委员会审查的不再是此前的大多数人道供应合同，而主要是含有《物品审查清单》所列项目的合同。不能拿一个固定的审批画面，覆盖整个计划的年月。[1]
这些细节不只是手续上的麻烦。放宽哪一道，保留哪一道，可能影响东西什么时候到、能到什么。反过来，若货物没有资金或没有运到，仅仅增加一个获批合同，也不能替生活增加同等数量的保障。
食品配给确实帮助许多人维持生活。这不能因为计划处在制裁之中，就被说成全无价值。但人并不是一张只要填够热量就能结清的表。能领到配给，与能靠自己的收入买到合适食物、维持工作和照料家人，是不同的生活。
2003年9月，粮农组织与世界粮食计划署的实地评估特别区分了食物供应和人们取得食物的能力：市场或国内生产有食物，不等于家庭有购买力。报告也把战争、制裁、干旱与经济衰败放在一起讨论，而不是只用一个原因解释所有困难。[4]
这里有一个不能互相顶替的区别：有人把粮食送来了，值得肯定；一个社会为什么需要如此依赖配给，仍值得追问。承认前者，不要求我们停止后者。指出后者，也不要求我们轻看那些真正送到的东西。
生活的修复往往比物资表更长。供水、电力、医疗和收入相互牵连。多一些食物可能很重要，却不能独自让一个损坏的生活网络恢复运转。这不是拒绝救助，而是别把救助已经做的部分，写成其余部分也都完成了。
## 不借一个站不住的数字说话
伊拉克制裁最著名、也最容易被不加核查地重复的争论之一，是儿童死亡。2000年，阿里与沙阿依据1999年调查发表研究，报告中南部儿童死亡率在战争和制裁时期显著上升。这是当时产生广泛影响的研究结论，不能假装它从未存在。[5]
但它也不能原封不动地当作今天已经核定的损失总账。2017年，戴森与切托雷利比较战后几项家庭调查，发现它们不支持此前所称长期大幅上升的走势，并提出1999年中南部数据受到操纵的严重判断。这是有论证的研究批评，需要标明是谁、何时提出，不能悄悄换成一项法院已经认定的事实。[6]
因此，这里不拿一个惊人的儿童死亡总数替整篇文章说话，也不把后来的质疑倒放进1991年，让当时的人仿佛已经知道后来所有研究。较新的分析使某个常用数字站不住，不等于战争、经济限制和生活困难便从来没有发生。
更不能从一段恶化，直接算出其中每一份损失有多少属于制裁、多少属于战争破坏、政府选择或其他条件。拒绝伪装精确，不是拒绝查责任；恰恰是要求责任的每一步，都能拿出相应证据。
不用一个宏大的数字，我们仍可以问一个具体问题：收到配给的人，能不能以自己受到的影响为理由，请一个独立的地方审查对他的安排？
在这里援引的制裁决议与物资申请程序中，能找到国家报告、合同申请、审查与付款；申请经常由常驻使团或联合国机构递交。它们没有因此成为让普通居民直接就全面制裁对自己的损害提起诉讼、取得赔偿裁判的个人法庭。[2][7]
这不等于所有人都不能说话。研究者可以调查，援助机构可以报告，国家可以要求调整，居民也并非完全没有表达。但让别人替你报告困难，与自己能启动一项会处理你请求的程序，仍有不同。这里讨论的是后一条路，并非宣布世界上不存在其他声音。
也不宜用后来卡迪案里的个人除名程序，替这段历史补上一扇原本没有的门。一整套贸易限制中的居民，并不是一张反恐名单上可以逐个申请移除的名字。措施变得更有针对性，或许能减少某些外溢成本，却会提出另一种问题：为什么偏偏是这个人？
所以，与卡迪并读，不是说我们已经找到从坏制裁走向好制裁的一条直线。两种措施针对的对象、施加压力的方法与能够利用的法律秩序都不同。要比较的是人怎样进入决定，又怎样有机会要求决定重新面对自己。
一袋面粉能够穿过制裁抵达，需要很多人把事情做成。它到达时，可以是一份真实的支持。但饭桌不是整段路的终点。坐在桌边的人仍能问：这样的生活为什么落到我身上，哪些限制还必要，谁能听取我的理由，谁有能力改变它？
body_en: The first food shipments under the Oil-for-Food Programme reached Iraq in March 1997. Its name suggests a short transaction: oil goes out, food comes in. Between those movements lay an international arrangement deciding how a country could use part of its own export earnings.[1]

Oil sales had to be authorized. Revenue passed into a UN-administered escrow account. Applications for supplies went through the relevant procedures before goods could arrive and be distributed. This was not simply a consignment of donated grain. The programme was principally financed by the sale of Iraqi oil.[3]

Following a bag of flour along that route opens several questions. Who allowed it through? Who controlled the money? Who was responsible for delivery? And what route could someone travel in the other direction, from a difficulty at the kitchen table back to the decision shaping it?
Food reaching a household matters. A household being able to initiate examination of the arrangement affecting it is another achievement. Neither should be used as a substitute for the other.
## A decision addressed to states enters daily life

The account cannot begin with Iraq only as the recipient of sanctions. Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990. On 6 August, the Security Council adopted Resolution 661 under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, imposing trade and financial restrictions to secure withdrawal and restore Kuwait’s legitimate authority. The invasion belongs in any account of the pressure that followed.[2]

The resolution contained exceptions for strictly medical supplies and, in humanitarian circumstances, food. It was not a text prohibiting every medicine and every meal. But an exception on paper is not yet access in practice. Money, permissions, transport and usable facilities lie between a permitted supply and someone being able to benefit from it.[2]

States implemented the restrictions through the transactions, territory and transport they could control. That does not make the international decision merely decorative. Its force reached people through national action. Equally, the common origin does not remove the need to examine what a particular implementing authority actually did.

The arrangement has to be read in both directions. What did the common decision require? What did each implementer add, permit, delay or refuse? Responsibility becomes harder to locate when every part can describe itself as only one link. That is a reason to trace the links, not a reason to give up.

After the 1991 war, a UN inter-agency mission warned of an impending humanitarian catastrophe. Iraq’s government declined the limited oil-sale proposals offered that year. Resolution 986 established Oil-for-Food in 1995; implementation arrangements were agreed in 1996, and oil exports began that December. Food followed in 1997.[3]

Those intervals were not empty time. A programme eventually starting does not show that earlier needs were met promptly. Iraq’s refusal of earlier proposals also cannot be removed to make the history a sequence of choices made entirely by outsiders. Each party’s decisions must stay available for examination.

Economic pressure can have a serious rationale when a state has invaded a neighbour and doing nothing is unacceptable. It can also be proposed as an alternative to further military action. Yet the absence of bombing from a particular measure does not establish an absence of costs. Whether pressure exists and who mainly bears it are different questions.
## Food is necessary; a life needs more

The programme joined controlled oil revenue to humanitarian imports. Its delivery arrangements differed by region: the Iraqi government implemented the programme under UN observation in the centre and south; the UN implemented it in the three northern governorates. Treating every distribution as the act of one undifferentiated institution loses the actual division of work.[3]

Even within a supply programme, approval, funding and arrival are different stages. The UN’s 2003 summary distinguished approved contracts, goods delivered, and supplies still in production or transit. It also described dependence on oil prices and export conditions. A contract approval cannot be counted as food already available to eat.[1]

Nor was approval organized identically throughout the period. A new procedure in 2002 sent contracts containing Goods Review List items to the sanctions committee, rather than continuing the earlier circulation of most humanitarian supply contracts. The system changed over time; one fixed picture of its paperwork will not explain the whole history.[1]

These differences determine what an improvement can mean. A faster approval can help without solving a funding gap. Funds can exist without goods having arrived. Goods can arrive without every other service needed for their use being restored. Each step deserves its own account of what happened.

Rations helped people sustain their lives. Their value does not vanish because they were supplied within a sanctions regime. Yet a person is not a column of calories waiting to be filled. Obtaining a ration and earning enough to choose an adequate diet are different ways of living, even when both prevent immediate hunger.

A September 2003 FAO/WFP assessment distinguished the availability of food from households’ capacity to obtain it. Supplies in markets or domestic production did not ensure purchasing power. Its account discussed war, sanctions, drought and economic deterioration together. It is evidence of interacting pressures, not an instrument for assigning every deprivation to one cause.[4]

There is no need to choose between appreciating a delivery and asking why reliance on deliveries became so extensive. The first recognizes work that helped. The second keeps the conditions of life open to scrutiny. Aid can have real value without answering every question about the system in which it is needed.

Recovery also reaches beyond an import ledger. Water, electricity, health services and income connect to one another. More food can be indispensable without repairing the whole network. Calling that limitation to attention is not a refusal of assistance. It is a refusal to report the unfinished parts as complete.
## An argument should not depend on an unreliable number

Child mortality became one of the most influential and contested parts of the sanctions debate. A 2000 article by Ali and Shah, based on the 1999 surveys, reported a substantial increase in childhood mortality in central and southern Iraq during the period following the Gulf conflict and under sanctions. That was an influential contemporary conclusion.[5]

In 2017, Dyson and Cetorelli compared later household surveys and found that they did not support the earlier picture of a large, sustained rise. They argued that the 1999 centre/south data had been manipulated. This is a serious research challenge, with authors, evidence and a date—not a judicial finding that an essay can silently treat as a verdict.[6]

The historical account therefore cannot rest on repeating a spectacular total of children said to have died because of sanctions. Nor can the later critique be handed backward to people making decisions in 1991. Evidence changes what can responsibly be claimed now; it does not give everyone in the past the same knowledge.

Rejecting an unreliable estimate does not establish that economic restrictions, war damage or hardship never existed. Conversely, establishing hardship does not calculate the share of each loss attributable to sanctions, destroyed infrastructure, government choices or other conditions. Refusing false precision should make an inquiry more demanding, not make responsibility disappear.

Without borrowing a vast number, a more specific question remains. Could someone receiving a ration initiate an independent examination of how the comprehensive restrictions affected that person? To ask this is not to presume that every claim would succeed. It is to ask where a claim could be considered.

The resolution and supply procedures cited here provide for state reports, applications, review and payments. Applications for humanitarian imports were submitted through permanent or observer missions and UN agencies. These arrangements did not establish a personal damages tribunal in which an ordinary resident could litigate the injury attributed to the comprehensive sanctions themselves.[2][7]

That is a narrower claim than saying that nobody could speak. Researchers investigated, agencies reported, and governments could press for changes. Public expression and advocacy can matter. But someone else reporting a hardship is not the same as the affected person being able to initiate a procedure empowered to address a particular request.

Nor should a later delisting procedure be inserted into this history as if it had always offered every resident an exit. A population living under comprehensive trade restrictions is not a collection of named entries on a counterterrorism list. Removing one name and reconsidering the effects of a trade regime are different institutional tasks.

The Kadi companion follows the other problem. A more targeted restriction may reduce some broad costs while concentrating coercion on a named individual. That makes the question of why this person was chosen more urgent, not unnecessary. Targeting is not itself proof that the target is right.

The two essays do not describe a straightforward ascent from bad sanctions to good ones, or a proven single causal path of institutional evolution. They examine different measures and different routes to review. Who can bring a question, before whom, and with what possible effect? The answers have to be found rather than supplied by the label.

A bag of flour reaching a household is a real achievement by people who enabled it to arrive. But the kitchen table need not be the end of the route. The person sitting there can still ask why life has taken this form, which restrictions remain necessary, who will examine the reasons, and who can change the decision.
